Section A OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 152 Articles: 1
18 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 152
a OurBigBook.com
A is poly(norbornene); B is the corresponding sequential block copolymer with a methyl-ester-substituted second block. The process is ring-opening metathesis polymerization. Each strained bicyclic alkene becomes a cyclopentane unit whose two backbone attachment positions are joined to neighbouring units through −CH=CH− links. The second block retains its CO2​Me substituent on the cyclopentane framework. Thus a useful connectivity representation is end−[CH=CH−C5​H8​]n​−[CH=CH−C5​H7​(CO2​Me)]m​−end, with the cyclopentane attachment positions at 1 and 3. This representation specifies connectivity rather than a single backbone alkene geometry.
The ruthenium alkylidene reacts with a monomer alkene through a metallacyclobutane, then fragments with the other pair of bonds broken. A new ruthenium alkylidene remains at the growing end, allowing propagation and then addition of the second monomer. Relief of the bicyclic monomer's ring strain supplies the principal enthalpic driving force; the loss of monomer translational entropy opposes polymerization. Sequential addition yields blocks only if the first population of active ends survives until the second addition.

DPn​=[I]0​[M]0​​x=50(0.98)=49.​

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
A sufficiently phase-separated block copolymer can show two glass transitions, associated approximately with its two microdomains. Simultaneous feeding instead tends to distribute the monomers along each chain, giving a statistical copolymer and usually one composition-dependent glass transition. Different monomer reactivities could produce a gradient rather than a perfectly random sequence.
For a homogeneous mixture an approximate interpolation is the Fox equation, Tg−1​=w1​/Tg1​+w2​/Tg2​, with temperatures in kelvin. Two transitions are not guaranteed merely by block architecture: short blocks, miscibility or insufficient experimental resolution can give one broad transition. The contrast is between domain-specific segmental environments and a more uniform mixed environment.

Words: 147 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 147
d OurBigBook.com
C has a saturated backbone and pendant CH2​OH groups in its second block. Hydrogenation converts every backbone CH=CH to CH2​CH2​; lithium aluminium hydride then reduces each CO2​Me to CH2​OH. The resulting connectivity is [CH2​CH2​−C5​H8​]50​−[CH2​CH2​−C5​H7​(CH2​OH)]75​.
Hydrogenation removes local double-bond rigidity and commonly lowers the segmental barrier to motion, favouring a lower glass transition temperature. Ester reduction changes polarity and side-group volume, while the new hydroxyl groups introduce hydrogen bonding, which can raise the hydroxyl-rich block's glass transition temperature and strengthen segregation. These competing effects preclude a numerical transition shift or an unconditional direction for both transitions from structure alone.
The repeat-unit formulae after both operations are C7​H12​ and C8​H14​O. Taking standard atomic masses,
Mn,repeat​=50(96.173)+75(126.199)=1.4274×104 gmol−1.​
(2)
This is approximately 14.27 kg mol−1 plus the net end-group mass. The termination chemistry is unspecified, so a more precise whole-chain mass is not determined; the methyl group lost during ester reduction must not remain in the second repeat's mass.

e

Words: 130 Articles: 1
18 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 130
e OurBigBook.com
Pendant alcohols can form reversible borate bridges, schematically P−O−B(OH)−O−P′ and B(O−P)3​, where P and P′ belong to different chains. Tetrahedral borate species are also possible depending on pH and water content. A bridge must connect different network strands to act as a cross-link; an intrachain loop does not contribute equivalently to elasticity.
Between cross-links, stretching reduces the number of accessible chain conformations. A simple incompressible rubber elasticity model gives the nominal tensile stress
σnominal​=G(λ−λ−2),G≃νe​kB​T,​
(3)
where λ is the extension ratio and νe​ the density of elastically active strands. The initial response is soft; stronger extension gives increasing stress and ultimately finite-chain extensibility. Reversible borate exchange permits stress relaxation, rate dependence and a loading–unloading hysteresis loop, rather than permanent ideal elasticity at arbitrarily long times.

f

Words: 102 Articles: 1
18 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 102
f OurBigBook.com
Reductive ozonolysis cuts the unsaturated backbone into cyclopentane-1,3-dicarbaldehyde units, apart from end fragments. Both alkene carbons carry a hydrogen, so the carbonyl products are aldehydes rather than ketones. Ring substituent stereochemistry is inherited from the polymer repeat; backbone E/Z geometry does not survive cleavage.
Ozone adds across a backbone alkene by cycloaddition, giving a primary ozonide. Its fragmentation produces a carbonyl group and a carbonyl oxide, which recombine to a secondary ozonide. Dimethyl sulfide reduces the peroxide-containing intermediate, forming dimethyl sulfoxide and the two carbonyl termini. Repetition at every backbone double bond liberates the dialdehyde. An oxidizing work-up would instead risk oxidation to carboxylic acids, so the specified reductive work-up is essential.

a OurBigBook.com
Let R=CH2​CH(Ph)−O−TEMPO, so B is HO−R. Its hydroxyl group initiates ring-opening polymerization of lactide, giving
C=H−[OCH(Me)CO]2n​−O−CH2​CH(Ph)−O−TEMPO.​
(4)
Each lactide contributes two lactyl repeat units. Dry monomer, exclusion of water and an alcohol-compatible catalyst such as tin(II) 2-ethylhexanoate under heating provide a practical route. Alcohol/metal-alkoxide exchange followed by lactide coordination and acyl–oxygen cleavage extends the ester chain while retaining a terminal hydroxyl group.
Heating C under oxygen-free conditions homolytically cleaves its benzylic C–O bond to the nitroxide, releasing a benzylic radical and TEMPO. The radical adds styrene repeatedly; reversible trapping by TEMPO controls the active radical concentration. D is therefore a poly(lactide)–polystyrene block copolymer with junction PLA−OCH2​CH(Ph)−[CH2​CH(Ph)]m​−O−TEMPO and the hydroxyl end of PLA retained. This is nitroxide-mediated polymerization; a temperature around 120–130 °C is a representative condition for a TEMPO/styrene system, rather than an exact universal optimum.

b

Words: 102 Articles: 1
19 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 102
b OurBigBook.com
Styrene, benzoyl peroxide and TEMPO provide the required radical addition–trapping sequence. Heating the peroxide breaks its O–O bond into benzoyloxy radicals. Before decarboxylation, PhCO2∙​ can add to styrene's terminal carbon, generating the resonance-stabilized radical PhCO2​CH2​C˙HPh. Coupling with the oxygen-centred TEMPO radical then gives PhCO2​CH2​CH(Ph)−O−TEMPO, the benzoate-protected alkoxyamine A.
The connectivity distinguishes this route from initiators that leave a carbon-based radical fragment at the chain end. Competition with benzoyloxy-radical decarboxylation affects yield, so this is a plausible preparation rather than a claim of exclusive product formation. Subsequent benzoate cleavage reveals B's hydroxyl group without requiring rupture of its alkoxyamine linkage.

The ideal number-average molar mass is approximately 25.11 kg mol−1. Quantitative uptake of 100 lactide and 100 styrene molecules per bifunctional initiator gives
Mn​=MB​+100Mlactide​+100Mstyrene​≃277.41+100(144.13)+100(104.15)=25105.4 gmol−1.​
(5)
B has formula C17​H27​NO2​. Lactide's entire cyclic diester mass is incorporated; multiplying its molar mass by two again would double-count its two lactyl units. The estimate assumes quantitative initiation, conversion, nitroxide recapping and no chain transfer or loss of chain-end fragments.

d

Words: 142 Articles: 1
19 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 142
d OurBigBook.com
Hydroxide attacks a PLA ester carbonyl, moving the π electrons onto oxygen. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate expels an alkoxide; proton transfer produces an alcohol and a carboxylate. The carboxylate stabilizes the hydrolysis products and makes this saponification effectively irreversible under the basic conditions. Repetition cleaves the PLA block, including its terminal ester linkage to the junction alcohol, while the carbon–carbon polystyrene backbone remains intact.
The principal surviving polymer is a polystyrene chain bearing the junction HOCH2​CH(Ph)− end and its nitroxide-derived distal end. In gel permeation chromatography, the intact block copolymer normally elutes earlier than this smaller surviving polystyrene coil. Lactate and short hydrolysis fragments elute later still, provided the column and detector resolve such small solutes. The polymer peak therefore shifts to larger elution volume; its height need not remain constant under a mass-sensitive detector. Elution reflects hydrodynamic volume, so calibration against polystyrene standards does not supply an exact absolute mass for the original mixed block.

e

Words: 105 Articles: 1
19 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 105
e OurBigBook.com
Replacing lactide by ethylene oxide gives
HO−[CH2​CH2​O]50​−CH2​CH(Ph)−[CH2​CH(Ph)]100​−O−TEMPO.​
(6)
The first chain grows by alkoxide attack on ethylene oxide, followed by protonation at work-up; the alkoxyamine subsequently controls styrene polymerization. The final material is an amphiphilic block copolymer. In water, polystyrene avoids solvent exposure while the poly(ethylene oxide) block is hydrated. Above a concentration-dependent assembly threshold, micelles with a polystyrene core and hydrated poly(ethylene oxide) corona are a reasonable morphology. Unimers remain in equilibrium with aggregates. Core–corona assembly lowers unfavourable water contact but costs chain-stretching and translational entropy. Block volume fractions, solvent history and concentration can instead favour cylinders or vesicles, so the chemical structure alone does not uniquely establish spherical micelles.

Solution
Words: 112
a OurBigBook.com
Place the trigonal axis along z, the axial ligands on ±z and the equatorial ligands in the xy plane. The ordering is e′′(dxz​,dyz​)<e′(dxy​,dx2−y2​)<a1′​(dz2​). The e′′ pair has nodal behaviour along both the equatorial ligand directions and the axial axis, minimizing direct ligand repulsion. The in-plane e′ pair points into the equatorial region. The dz2​ lobes point at both axial ligands and its torus also samples the equatorial ligands, giving the largest repulsion in the regular point-charge geometry.
Rotation by 120° and reflection in the equatorial plane preserve the geometry; they enforce the indicated doublet degeneracies. The ordering concerns a regular trigonal bipyramid with equivalent ligand-field assumptions, not every distorted five-coordinate complex.

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
For two independent identical ions at sufficiently high temperature, Curie's law gives χT=2(NA​μB2​/3kB​)g2S(S+1). In the cgs units used here, NA​μB2​/3kB​≃0.125 cm3Kmol−1.
Fe(II), Co(II) and Ni(II) have S=2, 3/2 and 1, respectively. The corresponding high-spin occupancies, ordered as (e′′,e′,a1′​), are
FeII:d6=(3,2,1),CoII:d7=(4,2,1),NiII:d8=(4,3,1).​
(7)
Hund filling puts one electron in each orbital before additional pairing. Spin-only dimer values at g=2 would be 6.0, 3.75 and 2.0; the observed larger values anticipate orbital contributions. The spin assignments require the chemically appropriate high-spin states, rather than rounding the measured χT directly to a spin-only integer.
ii
Words: 90 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 90
ii OurBigBook.com
Using the spin values above and accounting for two metal ions per formula unit,
gFe​=7.4/1.5​=2.22,gCo​=5.2/0.9375​=2.36,gNi​=3.4/0.5​=2.61.​
(8)
The deviations from 2 indicate spin-orbit coupling and incomplete quenching of orbital angular momentum. The partly filled e′′ manifold in Fe and e′ manifold in Ni permit orbital degeneracy in the ideal geometry. Co's high-spin orbital occupation is more orbitally balanced, but mixing with excited ligand-field states still produces a substantial effective g shift. These fitted scalar values summarize a thermally averaged response; they do not determine the individual components of an anisotropic g tensor.

i OurBigBook.com
The radical's magnetic orbital has π symmetry. Fe(II)'s partly occupied e′′ set supplies a matching metal π magnetic orbital, permitting electron transfer and predominantly antiferromagnetic metal–radical exchange. In Co(II) and Ni(II), that set is filled; their unpaired metal electrons occupy orbitals of different symmetry. Approximate orthogonality suppresses the usual antiferromagnetic kinetic-exchange pathway, favouring ferromagnetic metal–radical coupling through the remaining exchange contributions.
This orbital-symmetry argument assumes the intended idealized binding geometry. It predicts exchange signs, not exact magnitudes; distortion and additional orbital mixing can alter the competition.

Adopt H=−2J(S1​+S2​)⋅s−2J′S1​⋅S2​, with S1​=S2​=1 and ligand spin s=1/2. Let S12​=S1​+S2​ and S=S12​+s. The angular momentum addition identities give
E=−J{S(S+1)−S12​(S12​+1)−3/4}−J′{S12​(S12​+1)−4}.
(9)
The five allowed multiplets are
S12​01122​S1/21/23/23/25/2​E4J′2J+2J′−J+2J′3J−2J′−2J−2J′​​
(10)
Their degeneracies 2,2,4,4,6 sum to 18, matching 3×3×2. For dominant ferromagnetic J, the ground multiplet has S12​=2, S=5/2. A weak antiferromagnetic J′ does not overcome the two strong metal–radical bonds.

Words: 120 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 120
iii OurBigBook.com
A frustrated triangle has two ferromagnetic metal–radical bonds and an antiferromagnetic metal–metal bond. With the Hamiltonian convention above, take J/kB​=+800 K and J′/kB​=−8 K. In the maximally aligned ground state the two metal–radical products are 1×1/2 and the metal–metal product is 1×1. Therefore
FC​=−2(800)(1/2)+82(800)(1/2)−8​=−808792​=−0.9802.​
(11)
Here FC​=−1 denotes complete satisfaction of all exchange interactions; the small deviation 1+FC​=0.0198 quantifies the weak frustrated contribution in this normalization. The numerical answer assumes antiferromagnetic metal–metal exchange. The printed magnitudes alone do not establish that sign. If the metal–metal exchange were instead ferromagnetic, all three bonds would be satisfied and FC​=−1. The ground-state scalar products also follow directly from S12​=2, S=5/2, so a separate classical approximation is unnecessary for this fully polarized multiplet.

For an axial spin Hamiltonian HD​=DSz2​ with D/kB​=−25 K, the minima are mS​=±5/2. The highest levels along the reversal ladder are the mS​=±1/2 doublet. Hence
U/kB​=∣D∣{(5/2)2−(1/2)2}=25(6)=150 K,​
(12)
about 1.25 kJ mol−1 or 12.9 meV per molecule. Using ∣D∣S2 would incorrectly put a half-integer spin at a nonexistent mS​=0 level. Transverse anisotropy and quantum tunnelling of magnetization can create faster relaxation pathways, so this axial ladder barrier need not equal an experimentally fitted effective barrier.

Words: 98 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 98
ii OurBigBook.com
Frequency-dependent ac susceptibility probes relaxation: a peak in the out-of-phase component occurs approximately when ωτ=1. Measuring its displacement with frequency determines τ(T); an activated region may fit τ=τ0​exp(Ueff​/kB​T). A low-temperature departure can reveal tunnelling or other relaxation channels.
Low-temperature, sweep-rate-dependent magnetization hysteresis tests whether reversal is slow on the measurement timescale. A loop opening below the blocking temperature, variation with sweep rate and possible tunnelling steps provide complementary evidence. Isothermal remanent magnetization decay after field removal directly measures the associated relaxation time. A single open loop alone would not distinguish isolated-molecule blocking from collective ordering or impurities.

a OurBigBook.com
The framework is a three-dimensional network of corner-connected MO6​ octahedra, with each apparent corner connection extended through a bridging formate, M−O−CH−O−M. Each metal is coordinated by six oxygen donors from six formates, which link it to six neighbouring metals in the perovskite-like topology. The guanidinium cation occupies the larger cavity and can hydrogen-bond to formate oxygen atoms. Charge balance is +1+2−3=0.

b

Words: 97 Articles: 1
21 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 97
b OurBigBook.com
At high temperature, approximately independent paramagnetic ions give the appropriate Curie constant. The negative Weiss temperatures and the reduction of χT on cooling initially indicate predominantly antiferromagnetic correlations. The sharp rise near the ordering temperature nevertheless reveals a strongly enhanced low-field magnetic response.
A net moment could arise from a canted antiferromagnet, a ferrimagnet, or a ferromagnet with competing antiferromagnetic interactions. Differences between field-cooled magnetization and zero-field-cooled magnetization suggest history-dependent domain selection or slow relaxation, but are not alone proof of a particular microscopic spin arrangement. An ordinary compensated antiferromagnet would not account for a large ordering-related ferromagnetic-like low-field contribution without an additional mechanism.

c

Words: 194 Articles: 1
21 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 194
c OurBigBook.com
Weak ferromagnetism from canted antiferromagnetic order is the consistent model. Importantly, the plot has different magnetization scales: the left axis belongs to Mn and Fe; the right belongs to Co and Ni. Approximate low-temperature field-cooled readings are 40, 50, 450 and 390 G cm3 mol−1, respectively. Dividing by 5585 gives
MFC​≃(0.0072, 0.0090, 0.081, 0.070) μB​ per metal.​
(13)
These moments are tiny compared with fully aligned moments of about 5.09, 4.40, 4.25 and 2.47 μB​, calculated using the Curie-derived g values below. A conventional ferromagnet of the full high-spin ions would have much larger spontaneous magnetization; a simple bipartite array of identical metal sites also supplies no obvious unequal sublattice moments for ferrimagnetism. Opposed large sublattice moments with a small transverse uncompensated component reconcile the net response with negative Θ.
If the 10 Oe field has aligned the weak-ferromagnetic domains, Mweak​=gSμB​sinα estimates sublattice canting angles of roughly 0.08°, 0.12°, 1.1° and 1.6°. These are illustrative, not precision structure determinations: the low field may not fully align the domains, and the readings are graphical. Bulk magnetization strongly supports this model but does not uniquely establish every spin direction; magnetic neutron diffraction would test the microscopic arrangement.

Words: 126
d OurBigBook.com
Use C=0.125g2S(S+1) for one ion per formula unit, with high-spin S=5/2,2,3/2,1 for Mn, Fe, Co, Ni. Then
g≃(2.04, 2.20, 2.83, 2.47).​
(14)
High-spin Mn(II), with an approximately orbitally nondegenerate d5 ground state, stays closest to the free-electron value. Fe, Co and Ni have stronger orbital admixture, particularly Co in this effective Curie-law comparison. Spin-orbit coupling creates magnetic anisotropy, which can make reversal of the weak-ferromagnetic domains slower and enhance field-cooled/zero-field-cooled separation. A field-cooled sample selects domains as it orders; a zero-field-cooled sample initially has competing domains and can remain pinned when a small measuring field is applied.
This is a qualitative rationalization, not a strict proportionality between g−2 and the magnetization separation. The anisotropy tensor, domain-wall pinning and experimental timescale also matter; scalar g values alone do not quantitatively fix the divergence.

Below the ordering temperature, coherent spin correlations produce magnetic Bragg intensity. Depending on the magnetic propagation vector, this can appear as additional peaks or as added intensity at positions already occupied by nuclear reflections. A magnetic unit cell larger than the chemical one gives extra reciprocal-space positions; a zero-propagation-vector canted structure need not do so.
Magnetic intensity generally decreases at large scattering vector through the magnetic form factor and depends on moment components perpendicular to the scattering vector. Above the transition the long-range magnetic Bragg contribution disappears, though short-range correlations can leave diffuse scattering. The nuclear pattern remains approximately unchanged unless magnetic ordering also drives a structural distortion.

In electrophoresis, an applied electric field drives a charged particle and its associated diffuse ionic atmosphere relative to the liquid. Electric forcing is balanced by viscous stresses, giving a steady velocity v=μe​E in the linear regime. The relevant electrokinetic potential is the zeta potential at the slipping plane, rather than necessarily the solid surface potential.
For a thin electric double layer, the surrounding layer develops an electro-osmotic flow and the Smoluchowski electrophoretic mobility is μe​=ϵζ/η. The sign of ζ fixes the direction. This transport is different from dielectrophoresis, which can move a neutral polarizable particle in a nonuniform field.

and therefore v=3.13×10−5 m s−1, along the field for the positive zeta potential.

The amphiphile packing parameter is p=v/(aℓ): hydrocarbon volume divided by the product of effective head-group area and maximal tail length. For a spherical core of radius R, v/a=R/3; requiring R≤ℓ gives spheres for p≲1/3. Cylindrical cores instead have v/a=R/2, favouring cylinders or rods for roughly 1/3<p≲1/2. Lower-curvature bilayer structures are favoured towards p≃1; intermediate ranges can include flexible or closed bilayer morphologies.
The charged sulfate head groups make the effective area sensitive to electrostatic repulsion, salt and counterion binding. Screening can reduce that area, increasing p and favouring growth from spheres towards elongated micelles. These are geometric selection rules, not exact phase boundaries or a claim that every morphology is stable at any concentration.

A stable charge-stabilized dispersion has an interaction barrier large compared with kB​T. In DLVO theory, the total pair potential combines attractive Van der Waals forces with repulsion from overlapping electric double layers. Similar surface charges raise the free energy of overlap; a sufficiently high positive barrier prevents thermally diffusing particles from reaching the deep primary minimum near contact.
Other stabilization mechanisms include steric stabilization by solvated surface chains and combined electrosteric protection by charged chains. Such contributions are additional to the simplest DLVO pair potential. Increasing salt shortens the Debye length, so double-layer repulsion becomes shorter-ranged and the protective barrier can decrease.

Primary-minimum aggregation occurs when particles can cross the repulsive barrier and reach near contact. Its deep attractive well usually makes escape slow on experimental timescales, giving effectively irreversible coagulation. Higher electrolyte concentration screens the repulsion and can eliminate the barrier. The critical coagulation concentration is the electrolyte concentration at which rapid, approximately diffusion-limited coagulation sets in under the specified conditions; in an idealized DLVO description it is associated with loss of the protective barrier. Ion valence and surface boundary conditions strongly influence this threshold.

Secondary-minimum flocculation traps particles at a larger separation in a shallow attractive well. The primary barrier can remain intact, so particles form loose aggregates without reaching molecular contact. Such flocs are often reversible on dilution or a suitable change in ionic strength. If the secondary well is very weak compared with kB​T, the dispersion remains largely unassociated; if screening removes the primary barrier, the particles can proceed to the much deeper primary minimum. “Aggregation” and “flocculation” have variable usage, so the physical distinction here is explicitly shallow, separated association versus near-contact coagulation.

A depletion force requires mobile nonadsorbing polymers excluded from the gap, rather than grafted chains alone. If their depletion layers overlap when the plate separation is h<2δ, the overlap restores accessible solution volume and increases polymer entropy. For ideal, dilute depletants of bulk osmotic pressure Π, an idealized interaction free energy per plate area is
W(h)≃−Π(2δ−h)(0<h<2δ),W(h)≃0(h≥2δ).​

Its attractive pressure is −Π in the overlap interval. The layer thickness is of order the ideal-coil radius of gyration, δ∼Rg​=b0​N/6​, so the range scales as N1/2. Grafted brushes instead oppose compression through stretching and osmotic penalties; they can coexist with depletion attraction if free depletants are present, but the mere existence of a grafted layer does not create a reservoir of depleting chains. F=U−TS,Uconfigurational​=0,equilibrium maximizes accessible configurational entropy.​
(25)
The kinetic contribution is common to the phases at the same temperature. “Entropy-driven crystallization” does not mean that particles develop an energetic attraction; excluded volume changes the number of possible many-particle arrangements.

At high density, disorder can frustrate efficient local packing and leave particles with very little room to move. An ordered arrangement can give every particle a larger cage of allowed displacements. The extensive gain in vibrational/configurational freedom within these cages can outweigh the loss of distinct spatial arrangements of cages. Visual order is therefore not a reliable measure of entropy. At low density the fluid's freedom to rearrange dominates, whereas sufficiently dense packing can favour a crystal through accessible free volume.

  • −18: minima 8 and 9, whose exact connecting barrier is −19.
  • −14: minima 6 and 7.
  • −8: minima 2 and 3.
  • 2: minima 4 and 5, whose exact barrier is 0.25.
  • 6: the 2–3 and 4–5 groups join through the barrier of 5.
  • 8: the 6–7 group joins the 2–3–4–5 group.
  • 10: minimum 1 joins that group.
  • 12: the 8–9 group joins the rest.
These eight merges connect all nine minima without duplicating a basin. Minimum endpoints lie at their stated energies; branch heights are the discretized superbasin thresholds, not necessarily the exact saddle energies. A hydroxyl-directed Evans–Saksena reduction gives the required anti-1,3-diol. A suitable reagent is tetramethylammonium triacetoxyborohydride in an acidic medium, for example acetic acid/acetonitrile. Ligand exchange between the pre-existing alcohol and an acetoxyborohydride group tethers the reducing reagent to the substrate. Intramolecular hydride delivery to the ketone then proceeds through a six-membered arrangement, converting C=O to an alkoxide while conserving all existing stereocentres. Hydrolysis releases the second hydroxyl group.
The preferred directed transition-state conformation minimizes crowding by the larger carbon-chain substituents. It delivers the new C–H bond on the face that leaves the two hydroxyl groups anti, as in B: with the original hydroxyl drawn as a wedge in the printed zigzag, the new hydroxyl is dashed. The intervening methyl stereocentre is retained. Choosing an undirected borohydride reduction would not by itself rationalize this strong substrate-controlled relationship.

Dibutylboron triflate coordinates the imide carbonyl and triethylamine removes the propionyl α proton, giving predominantly the Z dibutylboron enolate. Its connectivity is Aux−N−C(O−BBu2​)=CHMe; the imide auxiliary remains attached, rather than being displaced during enolization. Coordination of cinnamaldehyde's oxygen to boron organizes a six-membered Zimmerman–Traxler transition state.
A chair with the aldehyde's styryl group pseudoequatorial avoids the auxiliary's bulky benzyl side. Formation of the C–C bond and transfer of the aldehyde oxygen into the boron coordination sphere give the boron aldolate, which hydrolyses to D. A Z enolate gives the syn aldol relationship. In the printed product zigzag, the labelled α-methyl bond should therefore be a solid wedge, on the same stereochemical face as the neighbouring solid-wedge hydroxyl bond. With the stated connectivity, the labelled carbon is R: priority is imide carbonyl, then CH(OH)CH=CHPh, then methyl, then hydrogen. The adjacent hydroxyl centre is S. Epoxidation of the hydroxyl-adjacent alkene is therefore favoured, even though both alkenes are in principle oxidizable. Peracid epoxidation is a concerted oxygen transfer: alkene π donation to terminal peroxide oxygen, O–O cleavage, proton transfer and carbonyl re-formation occur through a cyclic transition-state arrangement. The alkene's E geometry is retained as a trans relationship between its substituents in the epoxide.
The two alkene faces are diastereotopic because the molecule already contains stereocentres. A plausible substrate-controlled conformation minimizes allylic strain and presents the face opposite the bulky OTBS-bearing part of the chain to the oxidant. Hydrogen-bond direction, steric approach and conformational population compete; one cannot deduce an exact diastereomeric ratio from the flat drawing alone. Its tethered E alkene attacks the aldehyde-derived carbon through a chair-like six-membered arrangement: the alkene carbon farther from the alcohol forms the new C–C bond, placing a carbocation at the nearer alkene carbon. Trifluoroacetate captures that cation; the basic methanolic work-up cleaves the trifluoroacetate ester to reveal the ring hydroxyl group. This is a Prins cyclization.
Number the product ring from oxygen through the aldehyde-derived carbon as C2, then the alkene-derived methyl-bearing carbon C3, the hydroxyl-bearing carbon C4, the intervening methylene C5 and the original alcohol carbon C6. A chair keeping the bulky C2 side chain and C6 hydroxymethyl group equatorial predicts 2,6-cis substitution. Suprafacial alkene capture preserves the E-alkene-derived relationship, giving 2,3-trans between the C2 side chain and C3 methyl. Preferred equatorial trapping of the C4 cation gives 3,4-trans, hence the 2,4,6-cis arrangement of the substituent-bearing bonds in the favoured chair. In the printed flat-ring orientation, draw the C2 side chain, C4 hydroxyl and C6 hydroxymethyl behind the plane, and C3 methyl in front. Existing stereocentres in the aldehyde side chain and at C6 are retained; they anchor the absolute face of this assignment.

The first two operations invert the allylic hydroxyl group. Triphenylphosphine adds to the azodicarboxylate, generating the reagent pair that converts the alcohol into an alkoxyphosphonium leaving group. Benzoate displaces it with inversion at carbon, giving the inverted benzoate ester. Methoxide then cleaves that ester by nucleophilic acyl substitution, retaining the newly inverted carbon–oxygen stereochemistry because cleavage occurs at the acyl group, not by substitution at the stereogenic carbon.
The inverted allylic alcohol exchanges with the orthoacetate under acid catalysis. Ethanol loss produces an allyl ketene acetal, schematically CH2​=C(OEt)−O−(allyl). A six-membered suprafacial Johnson-Claisen rearrangement breaks the allylic C–O bond, shifts the ring alkene by one position and forms the new bond from the original alkene terminus to the ketene-acetal CH2​. The result is the −CH2​CO2​Et substituent at the carbon that was the remote end of the original double bond. A chair-like transition state placing the larger substituents away from axial crowding explains the stereochemical transfer; the inverted alcohol configuration selects the corresponding face.
Finally, TiCl4​ activates the anomeric methoxy group and methoxide departure creates an oxocarbenium ion. Hydride transfer from triethylsilane replaces that methoxy substituent by hydrogen. The ring oxygen and pendant OTBS group remain intact. The sequence is inversion, stereospecific allylic rearrangement, then reductive removal of the anomeric methoxy group, rather than direct reduction or hydrolysis of the ester introduced by the Claisen step.

A consistent proposed sequence is desilylation, five-membered hemiketal formation, retro hetero-Diels–Alder opening, intramolecular aldol addition and hemiacetal closure. The essential carbon rearrangement is loss of the original ketone–side-chain bond and formation of a bond between its two neighbouring carbons; it is not a simple Michael addition.
For an explicit atom map, label the starting six-membered ring A−B=C−D−E−Or​−A, with the ketone at D, methyl substituents at A and B, the hydroxy group at A, and the side chain E−X−T−Et. Here X is the methylene and T is the carbon bearing the protected alcohol. Let OD​ be the original ketone oxygen and OT​ the protected alcohol oxygen. These labels identify atoms, not new substituents.
First, Fluoride removes the silyl protecting group from OT​. The resulting alcohol attacks the protonated ketone at D, forming the five-membered hemiketal D−E−X−T−OT​−D. The original oxygen OD​ is now a hydroxy group; the original pyran ring remains intact at this stage.
Next, The original pyran ring can undergo a retro hetero-Diels-Alder reaction. The three electron-pair movements are B=C→C=D, D−E→E=Or​ and Or​−A→A=B: break D−E and Or​−A, and form the three indicated double bonds. The result is the tethered aldehyde/dienol ester
MeCA​(OH)=CB​(Me)−CHC​=CD​(OH)−OT​−CHT​(Et)−CH2,X​−CHE​=Or​.
(42)
The temporary D−OT​ bond keeps both reacting ends within the same molecule. At D, both oxygen substituents remain attached, and the new D−OT​ tether prevents separation into independent fragments.
Then The C=D enol attacks the tethered aldehyde at E. Formation of C−E, restoration of D=OD​, and proton transfer give the six-membered lactone ring C−D−OT​−T−X−E−C, with E−Or​H. This is an intramolecular aldol reaction, and it supplies the crucial new carbon–carbon bond without losing any carbon atom.
Finally, Keto-enol tautomerism at A=B gives the methyl ketone at A and introduces the hydrogen at B. The E−Or​H alcohol then attacks that ketone, closing the five-membered hemiacetal ring A−B−C−E−Or​−A. The resulting fused rings have exactly the product's connectivity: D is the lactone carbonyl, OT​ is its ring oxygen, and Or​ is the five-membered-ring oxygen.
The stereocentre at T survives throughout this sequence. The configuration initially at E is erased at the aldehyde stage, and those at A, B, C and E arise during the later cyclization and proton-transfer steps. A folded intramolecular aldol reaction followed by reversible hemiacetal formation is consistent with the drawn cis ring junction, but connectivity and orbital bookkeeping alone do not prove that it is the unique selected diastereomer. In particular, a claim of simple retention at E would contradict this atom map.
A related pyranone-to-fused-lactone rearrangement under aqueous hydrogen fluoride is experimentally reported; that account also explicitly qualifies the relative stereochemistry as assigned on mechanistic grounds. The sequence above is a proposed explanation of the examination structure, rather than a mechanism claimed to have been experimentally established in that paper.[ref]

Solution
Words: 247
a OurBigBook.com
Use symmetric single-bead displacements with the Metropolis acceptance rule, discard equilibration, and record the end-to-end distance after complete sweeps, including sweeps with rejected moves. One sweep is N attempted bead moves; it is a sampling index, not physical time.
INITIALIZE(N, sigma):
    for i = 1,...,N:
        r[i] = ((i-1)*sigma, 0, 0)
    return r

ENERGY(r):
    for each pair i < j:
        if norm(r[i]-r[j]) < sigma:
            return infinity
    U = 0
    for i = 1,...,N-1:
        U += k/2 * (norm(r[i+1]-r[i])-sigma)^2
    return U

TRIAL(r):
    choose i uniformly from 1,...,N
    choose delta uniformly from [-a,a]^3
    r_trial = copy(r)
    r_trial[i] += delta
    return r_trial

ACCEPT(U, U_trial, beta):
    if U_trial == infinity:
        return false
    return log(uniform(0,1)) < min(0, -beta*(U_trial-U))

MAIN:
    r = INITIALIZE(N, sigma)
    U = ENERGY(r)
    for sweep = 1,...,n_equilibrate+n_produce:
        repeat N times:
            r_trial = TRIAL(r)
            U_trial = ENERGY(r_trial)
            if ACCEPT(U, U_trial, 1/(k_B*T)):
                r = r_trial
                U = U_trial
        if sweep > n_equilibrate:
            d_ETE = norm(r[N]-r[1])
            store d_ETE and update its histogram
    estimate autocorrelation and block uncertainties
The straight initial chain is nonoverlapping and has zero bond-stretching energy, but is not presumed to be an equilibrium configuration. Check relaxation from contrasting initial configurations and stationarity before production. The displacement scale may be tuned during equilibration and then held fixed. Every sweep may be recorded; correlations are handled in uncertainty estimates rather than pretending adjacent records are independent. If thinning is used, choose its spacing with reference to the measured autocorrelation time. Rejected states must still be sampled to retain their correct equilibrium residence weight.

For a chosen bead, the uniform displacement cube is inversion symmetric, so the proposal distribution satisfies q(X→Y)=q(Y→X). The target canonical density is π(X)∝exp[−βU(X)] for allowed configurations. With a(X,Y)=min[1,e−β(U(Y)−U(X))],
π(X)q(X,Y)a(X,Y)=q(X,Y)min[π(X),π(Y)]=π(Y)q(Y,X)a(Y,X).​
(43)
This proves detailed balance. Overlapping trials have zero target weight and are rejected. The proposal must retain rejected trials as self-transitions; repeatedly proposing until a nonoverlapping move appears would generally introduce a configuration-dependent proposal normalization and need a Hastings correction. Detailed balance establishes stationarity, while sufficient sampling also requires practical exploration of the accessible state space.

If kσ2≫kB​T, bond lengths remain near σ and temperature mostly changes the small bond-length fluctuations, not the distribution of angular conformations. The end-to-end distance therefore fluctuates over an expanded self-avoiding-coil distribution even at low temperature, with an approximate scale σ(N−1)ν and ν≃0.588 for sufficiently long three-dimensional chains.
For N=10, the scaling is qualitative and finite-chain effects matter. An equilibrated distance-versus-sweep trace is stationary, with correlated excursions; a histogram of that trace is a distinct plot, not a curve of probability density against simulation step. Neither the temperature in kelvin nor the spring constant is specified, so an exact histogram cannot be calculated. The illustrative figure compares like-for-like coil traces rather than asserting a unique numerical simulation result.

Compact conformations normally dominate, giving a smaller characteristic end-to-end distance than the high-temperature coil. At kB​T≫ϵ, attractive contact energies are weak compared with thermal fluctuations, so expanded coil-like conformations are favoured and the end-to-end distribution broadens towards larger distances. Strong short-range repulsion still limits overlap over an effective, temperature-dependent diameter. The soft Lennard-Jones model is therefore not exactly identical to a temperature-independent hard-sphere chain, even when attraction is relatively unimportant.
A sufficiently stiff spring keeps the chain contour length near (N−1)σ in all three comparisons. If temperature instead becomes comparable with kσ2/kB​, increased bond stretching introduces an additional size change and the intended fixed-bond coil comparison breaks down. Every equilibrated trace should fluctuate around a stationary distribution; an expanding running mean caused by incomplete relaxation is not evidence for an equilibrium high-temperature state.

C has adjacent Cu sites and adjacent Li sites; in the conventional Gilman dimer D2​, Cu and Li alternate around the four metal positions. D is represented by Li[Cu(TMP)2​] per formula unit. Each Cp∗Al fragment leaves two electrons after allocating one aluminium valence electron to its monovalent cyclopentadienyl ligand. Four fragments therefore give eight cluster electrons. In the tetrahedral arrangement, fragment lone-pair/donor and vacant acceptor orbitals combine into delocalized cluster orbitals. The occupied low-energy set has a12​t26​ symmetry, analogous to a filled 1S and 1P shell; higher combinations remain empty. This is a multicentre description, not six independent two-electron Al–Al bonds, which would require twelve electrons.
A schematic molecular-orbital diagram should show the occupied nondegenerate a1​ level below the occupied triply degenerate t2​ set, separated from the empty higher levels. Detailed energies and ordering of the empty levels require an orbital calculation. On descending Group 13, stabilization of the ns2 pair and reduced favourable s–p mixing can weaken the tendency towards the same compact Al-like bonding pattern; metal–metal distances and preferred aggregation change. Ligand size, donor/acceptor properties and hapticity also tune fragment orbital energies and steric access, so neither substitution of the metal nor of Cp* is electronically innocent.

Eight AlMe vertices form a cube, five faces are capped by μ4​-C(Et) units, and the sixth face is capped by a bridging hydride. Choosing the hydride face as the bottom gives four equivalent side carbon caps and one distinct opposite carbon cap. Their ethyl groups give the 4:1 integrations: four methyl groups contribute 12 H and their methylenes 8 H; the remaining ethyl gives 3 H and 2 H.
The eight aluminium-bound methyl groups divide into two sets of four: the four aluminium atoms bordering the hydride face and the four on the opposite face. Each set gives a 12-proton singlet. The single bridging hydride gives the remaining one-proton signal. This matches the complete integration pattern without postulating five inequivalent ethyl caps. It specifies the symmetry-compatible connectivity; NMR alone does not measure every bond length or rule out solution averaging of small distortions.

Words: 116
ii OurBigBook.com
Use the neutral-fragment skeletal count: each AlMe supplies two electrons, each CEt supplies three and the bridging H supplies one. Hence
Nskeletal​=8(2)+5(3)+1=32=16 pairs.​
(52)
There are 13 nonhydrogen skeletal vertices, eight Al plus five C, and 16=n+3 pairs. In the usual PSEP classification this is therefore arachno, corresponding to a 15-vertex closo parent with two vertices absent. The μ4​-H cap contributes an electron but is not counted as a carbon-like skeletal vertex. The aluminium cube is a convenient subframework; its eight corners alone are not the complete Wade skeleton. Calculations on capped cubic carbaalanes likewise identify 16 skeletal pairs for the five-carbon-cap/one-hydride-cap case.[ref]

Words: 359 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 359
iii OurBigBook.com
The requested equality is 32 electrons if each unsaturated C=CHPh unit is counted as a four-electron donor to the chosen extended cluster framework. It needs that additional convention; a count confined to the localized Al7​C5​ skeleton gives 28 instead.
For B, an AlR fragment contributes two skeletal electrons, a singly substituted cap CR contributes three, and the bridging hydrogen contributes one:
NB​=8(2)+5(3)+1=32.
(53)
For the second formula, let x be the contribution assigned to each unsaturated unit. The comparison is
N=7(2)+3(3)+2x+1=24+2x.
(54)
Thus N=NB​ requires x=4. A bookkeeping partition that includes the two alkene π pairs in the extended cluster electron pool gives
Nextended​=7(2)+3(3)+2(2+2)+1=32.
(55)
In contrast, assigning the C=C double bond entirely to the exoskeletal substituent leaves each corresponding cage carbon with two electrons for the cage:
Nlocalized​=7(2)+3(3)+2(2)+1=28.
(56)
The difference is exactly the two π pairs, four electrons, rather than an arithmetic discrepancy. These are different electron partitions: do not compare 28 from one partition with 32 from the other as though both were the same skeletal count, and do not infer a structural classification merely by inserting the extended count into Wade's rules for twelve localized skeletal vertices.
Both the original and revised question pages print the same neutral molecular formula; the revised copy does not supply a charge, a drawing, or an explicit instruction about these π electrons.[ref] The primary study identifies the open cluster with the two genuine C=C groups and reports their hydroalumination to give the capped aluminium cube. Its accessible abstract does not establish the orbital partition needed to select the four-electron convention.[ref]
Conditional conclusion: the advertised 32-electron equality follows under the explicit extended-framework convention above. Without evidence that those π pairs belong in the cluster electron pool, retain the 28-electron localized count and this qualification. The source checks do not justify asserting a typo or inventing a charge to force agreement.

Solution
Words: 101
a OurBigBook.com
The product is 1,3,4-Oxadiazole. Protonation or phosphorylation activates one formyl carbonyl of the diacylhydrazine. The oxygen of the other carbonyl attacks intramolecularly, closing a five-membered ring containing the atom sequence O–C–N–N–C. Proton transfers and loss of water produce the conjugated ring; deprotonation restores the neutral aromatic heterocycle.
The overall transformation is C2​H4​N2​O2​→C2​H2​N2​O+H2​O. Polyphosphoric acid provides carbonyl activation and an acidic medium. P4​O10​ acts as a strong dehydrating agent, consuming water and maintaining the condensation-driving environment. Neither nitrogen is expelled, and the oxygen retained in the heterocycle originates from a carbonyl rather than an inserted reagent oxygen.

b

Words: 193 Articles: 1
34 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 193
b OurBigBook.com
The cyclic amino sugar equilibrates with its open-chain α-amino aldehyde. Two such units condense head-to-tail: each amino group adds to the other unit's aldehyde, followed by dehydration to the cyclic bis-imine/dihydropyrazine system. Formula accounting identifies the observed intermediate:
2(179)−2(18)=322.​
(57)
This corresponds to C12​H22​N2​O8​, so the accumulating intermediate has lost two waters but has not yet acquired the fully aromatic pyrazine oxidation state. The unchanged portions of both carbon chains become the substituents on opposite ring carbons.
Dehydrogenative aromatization gives B, retaining both hydroxylated side chains and releasing H2​: the intermediate loses two hydrogen atoms to reach C12​H20​N2​O8​, mass 320. A competing elimination of the hydroxyl group immediately adjacent to the ring in one side chain, with loss of a ring-adjacent proton, gives an exocyclic unsaturated intermediate. Proton transfers shift that unsaturation into the ring and leave a deoxygenated side-chain methylene. This dehydrative aromatization gives A, formally 322−18=304, rather than requiring a separate unexplained reducing agent. Both pathways gain aromatic stabilization, while only the dehydrogenative branch requires H2​ release. The acid/base proton-transfer steps can proceed through several tautomeric representations; mass balance distinguishes the two net branches.

The thioamide first undergoes sulfur alkylation at the bromomalonate carbon, displacing bromide. Intramolecular attack of nitrogen on one ester carbonyl and ethanol loss produce a five-membered thiazolinone-type intermediate. Tautomerization gives ethyl 2-(3-fluorophenyl)-4-hydroxythiazole-5-carboxylate. For unambiguous atom assignment, write the ring in order as S1–C2(aryl)–N3–C4(OH)–C5(CO2​Et): the thioamide carbon becomes C2, its nitrogen becomes N3, the attacked ester carbonyl becomes C4 and the original bromomalonate methine becomes C5.
Thus the correctly numbered intermediate is ethyl 2-(3-fluorophenyl)-4-hydroxythiazole-5-carboxylate. Triflic anhydride activates the hydroxyl oxygen; triethylamine removes its proton to give D = ethyl 2-(3-fluorophenyl)-4-(trifluoromethanesulfonyloxy)thiazole-5-carboxylate. This aryl triflate undergoes the subsequent palladium-catalysed alkynyl coupling at C4. The explicit ring atom mapping prevents interchanging the 4-hydroxy and 5-ester positions.

The acidic ethanolic step converts the terminal carboxylic acid to its ethyl ester, leaving the pre-existing thiazole ester. Azide then adds across the alkyne by 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition, followed by protonation at work-up. F contains an NH-1,2,3-triazole replacing the alkyne, with the thiazole and (CH2​)3​CO2​Et attached to its two carbon atoms. The thiazole's own CO2​Et group remains.
The formula check is decisive:
C18​H16​FNO4​S+C2​H4​+HN3​=C20​H21​FN4​O4​S.​
(58)
One can represent the cycloaddition with cyclic movement of the azide resonance-form electrons and the alkyne π electrons into the two new C–N bonds. Alkali azide initially gives a triazolide; aqueous work-up provides the NH. Interchanging formal 4/5 labels for the carbon substituents in an N-unsubstituted triazole does not establish a separate permanently fixed N-substituted regioisomer.

Words: 106
iii OurBigBook.com
KOH hydrolyses the thiazole ethyl ester to a carboxylate; acidification gives the acid. Silver(I) then activates the neighbouring alkyne towards intramolecular six-membered O-cyclization. The carboxylate oxygen attacks the alkyne carbon farther from the thiazole, so the new ring follows carbonyl C–O–distal alkyne C–proximal alkyne C–thiazole C4–thiazole C5. A vinyl-silver intermediate is protonated to give the fused pyrone G.
The remote terminal carboxylic acid survives. Ester hydrolysis changes E's formula by −C2​H4​ to C16​H12​FNO4​S; the subsequent addition across the alkyne changes connectivity without altering that formula. This distinguishes the lactonizing carboxyl group at thiazole C5 from the side-chain acid, which is not the group closing the observed fused ring.

Solution
Words: 122
iv OurBigBook.com
H is the fused pyridone analogue of G: replace the pyrone ring oxygen by NH, retaining its carbonyl and the remote carboxylic acid. Ammonia adds to the electron-poor pyrone system, opening its lactone/enol-ether framework into an amino-containing unsaturated acyl intermediate. Proton transfers permit intramolecular closure through nitrogen and loss of water, giving the conjugated pyridone/lactam ring. Acid work-up restores the neutral acid and the preferred neutral lactam representation.
The net atom change is +NH−O, so
C16​H12​FNO4​S⟶C16​H13​FN2​O3​S,​
(59)
exactly matching H. Merely forming a carboxamide from the terminal acid would remove a different oxygen and leave the pyrone oxygen intact; it would not explain the characteristic pyrone-to-pyridone ring transformation.

i OurBigBook.com
K is ethyl 4-(4-methylbenzoyl)-1H-pyrrole-2-carboxylate. AlCl3​ activates the aroyl chloride to an acylium-like electrophile. Pyrrole attacks through C4, forming a sigma complex; deprotonation restores aromaticity and work-up releases the ketone from its Lewis-acid complex.
Unsubstituted pyrrole normally favours an α position, but the ester at C2 changes the regioselectivity. Attack at C5, or at C3, permits important sigma-complex contributors with positive charge at the ester-bearing C2, which is strongly destabilized by the electron-withdrawing ester. C4 substitution avoids that particularly unfavourable contributor. The C2 ester therefore directs the acylation towards C4, overriding the simple unsubstituted-pyrrole rule. Combining the starting ester with a p-toluoyl group while replacing a ring hydrogen gives C15​H15​NO3​, as required.

Words: 105 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 105
ii OurBigBook.com
Sulfuryl chloride converts the aryl thiol into an electrophilic sulfur reagent, conveniently represented as ArSCl after chlorination and dehydrogenation. Triethylamine traps the generated acid. The pyrrole's two α positions are already occupied; its less deactivated remaining carbon, C4, attacks electrophilic sulfur, displacing chloride. Loss of the C4 proton restores the aromatic ring and gives the C4 arylthio-substituted pyrrole.
The net new bond is C(pyrrole)–S(aryl). Sulfur is retained from the thiol and becomes a thioether; the transformation is not sulfonylation by transfer of sulfuryl chloride's SO2​ group. Possible disulfide formation during thiol chlorination does not change the electrophilic-sulfenylation logic of the final ring substitution.

Solution
Words: 137
iii OurBigBook.com
Silver carbonate promotes deprotonation of the methylene group in methyl isocyanoacetate, giving the nucleophilic carbon MeO2​C−CH−−N≡C. It adds to the alkyne carbon farther from the electron-withdrawing sulfone. This creates the new bond between the future pyrrole C2 and methyl-bearing C3 and leaves the vinyl anion at the sulfone-bearing carbon, future C4.
The vinyl anion then attacks the terminal carbon of the isocyanide intramolecularly, closing a five-membered ring with atom sequence C2–C3–C4–C5–N. Proton transfers place one of the starting methylene hydrogens on nitrogen and the other on C5, giving an aromatic pyrrole. The product has CO2​Me at C2, methyl at C3 and the retained arylsulfonyl group at C4. This is an addition–cyclization–aromatization sequence: the isocyanide contributes both ring nitrogen and the otherwise unsubstituted ring carbon, rather than acting as a cyanide leaving group.
